A young woman stands as the focal point in the middle of a narrow, graffiti-covered urban alleyway, striking a playful, confident pose. She has long, colorful dreadlocks streaked with hot pink, magenta, teal, and green against natural blonde tones, and she holds a long-stemmed red rose horizontally across her lips with one hand while her other arm is raised, fingers resting lightly in her hair. Her outfit is edgy and street-style: a black cropped tank top exposing a toned midsection, very low-rise blue jeans heavily distressed with rips at the thighs and knees, cinched by a thin black belt, and chunky black platform boots with one foot crossed in front of the other. A delicate necklace and a simple bracelet add subtle detail. Behind her, two weathered red-brick buildings flank a tight passage whose walls are layered with stencils, spray-paint tags, and a large vivid floral mural on the left, alongside a graffiti-splattered metal drainpipe. The asphalt ground is marked with faded chalk drawings and paint, and the alley recedes toward a bright, overcast white sky, creating strong converging leading lines that draw the eye to her. The overall mood is a striking contrast of youthful vibrancy and color against gritty, textured urban decay.
Style: Urban street photography / fashion editorial portrait with a vibrant, graffiti-art cultural context
Composition: Full-body, centered vertical portrait at eye level; the parallel brick walls form symmetrical leading lines that converge on the subject, framing her in the dead center with the bright sky gap above
Lighting: Soft, even, diffused overcast daylight with no harsh shadows, producing gentle modeling on skin and fabric and allowing the saturated hair and rose to pop against the muted brick tones
Adjectives: edgy, vibrant, playful, gritty, confident

external.description:
Victoria Arellano had a gift with people. Her warm personality and ability to put people at ease had made her a vital resource at the drug and alcohol treatment facility she volunteered at, working with other people with HIV. When she was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcment (ICE), she brought this gift with her.

In her time at the San Pedro detention center she worked hard to comfort others.

And when she fell ill, those she was imprisoned with worked hard to return the favor offering her water, saving and peeling oranges for her when she was too ill to eat, and keeping watch on her when she grew sicker. They requested that Victoria receive her medication which her mother had tried to deliver to the detention center and demanded that she be seen by a doctor when it became clear that she wasn’t getting better.

Victoria never received her medication, Daposone, an antibiotic that helped prevent pulmonary infection like pneumonia, a common complication of HIV. Nor was she given a similar medication like Bactrium or any other treatment for her illness. Instead, she had been given Tylenol and later the antibiotic Amoxicillin for an UTI.

Yet Victoria needed far more than Tylenol or Amoxicillin and as she grew sicker the other detainees held with her grew angrier at the neglect.

When others at the detention center rioted, shouting hospital hospital,” Victoria was not taken to a hospital. Instead she was brought to another room in the facility where she reported being mocked and humiliated. By the time an ICE guard moved her head with his foot and asked what was wrong with her she had begun both urinating and vomiting blood for days. By the time she was taken to Little Company of Mary Hospital, it was too late. Victoria would die of untreated meningitis that had, in the words of her lawyer, “ _advanced that it involved her brain, her liver, her lungs, her heart, and a couple of other organs_ ” less than three months after entering ice detention. Her mother noted that she died minutes after ice removed the chains restraining her.

Victoria’s story may seem familiar to those following ice today even if her name does not. That’s because Victoria died in 2007, long before ICE developed their current reputation for medical neglect. Victoria was one of a disproportionate number of trans migrants to die in ICE detention before Operation Metro Surge.

Her death is also emblematic of how ICE treatment of trans people appears to herald future treatment of the general population. Maria Hinjosa makes a similar argument noting that it was Estrella, an undocumented trans woman, who was one of the first people ever taken from courtroom into ICE custody while she was seeking an order of protection from her abuser during the first Trump administration.

Over 60 people have died in ICE detention in the last year and hundreds have alleged medical neglect in ICE custody. Even more have been brought to hospitals with injuries inconsistent with the stories accompanying them like the man ICE argues ran into a wall headfirst.

Yet while the number of deaths has increased, Victoria’s case shows that medical neglect has long been apart of immigrant detention in the United States.

Recent coverage of the Folkston detention center where Luis Sandoval recently died notes that the DHS Office Of Inspector General found that conditions at FIPC “ _compromised the health, safety and rights of detainees_ ” in 2022. Yet this neglect is only an intensification of the dehumanization and abuse that migrants have faced for years according to multiple lawsuits and allegations leveled against ice since its creation in 2003.

Between 2003 and 2007, when Victoria died, 71 people had died in the agency’s custody.

Of these cases, a number revolve around trans migrants like Johana Medea Leon and Raxhana Hernandez, who died from what their families considered medical neglect in ice detention. Medical neglect is only one of the issues facing trans migrants in ice detention with many facing discrimination and sexual assault in detention after fleeing from anti-trans violence in their home countries, according to a Human Rights Report published in 2015.

Isa Noyola at the Transgender Law Center estimates that many in detention do not disclose their status for this reason even if they may have valid asylum cases and may need legal representation.

> “It is dangerous to disclose your trans identity [to ICE]. And for some people they have no choice, or like, they are outed.”

The Trump administration is no longer keeping statistics of the number of LGBT+ people detained making it harder for those detained to access legal services or for advocates to track discrimination or disparities in cases of abuse or neglect.

Kat Rohn at OutFront Minnestota which has been tracking the impacts of Operation Metro Surge argues that the huge upswing in violence seen during the surge builds on many years of dehumanization and abuse of trans and other migrants with trans women of color like Victoria Arellano bearing the brunt of the violence. She finds the lack of statistics particularly troubling,

> “Both the level of care has decreased dramatically, and the scrutiny over that from any sort of external parties, whether those are lawyers, whether those are advocacy organizations, whether those are you know any other groups that are having oversight over these spaces, has declined precipitously.”

> “And I think my largest concern in the current moment is that what we don't know is the real danger here. We know that people are being neglected and harmed in these facilities. We know that trans people, particularly trans women, have died in ICE facilities in the past because of this neglect, and we are deeply concerned that these same conditions are present and potentially even worse than they were during the sort of height of those very public recorded deaths during the last iteration of this administration.”

Yet, if Victoria’s case highlights the impacts of policies of disposability it also highlights its opposite. Namely, the humanity and the determination of the 80 men housed with Victoria that July in 2007. In the months following Victoria’s death, two other immigrants, Rosa Isela Contreras-Dominguez who was seven months pregnant at the time of her death and Edmar Alves Araujo, would die and calls to reform the then new immigration system would rise. Those reforms, on the whole, would not be put in place and even when they were, like when then-President Obama established more trans inclusive intakes for trans detainees advocates like Isa Noyola argues that they missed the point.

> “We don’t want rainbow colored cages.”

record.text: Regardless of generative AI's existence, LGBTQ+ artists have shown that they will create space to be heard and understood in their own communities.

external.description:
Sep. 23, a study was published in the Association for Computing Machinery’s journal on human computer-interaction titled I Just Don't Want My Work Being Fed Into The AI Blender": Queer Artists on Refusing and Resisting Generative AI. The study, written by authors Jordan Taylor, Joel Mire, Alicia DeVrio, Maarten Sap, Haiyi Zhu, and Sarah E. Fox, details how individuals of queer, trans and nonbinary communities feel about the rise of generative AI.

Ranging from game design, writing anthologies, and cosplay construction, to digital art trades, fan-made art books, and media design, queer artists from a range of different backgrounds come together to share their art.

Studies show that the history of trans and queer art influences what we create in present times, and the origins of queer art make sense of how generative AI affects the communities formed by LGBTQ+ art in the present.

When asked what made him question the impact of generative AI on queer artists, Jordan Taylor told The Needle via email that,

> “Researchers tend to think of LGBTQ+ communities as targets of bias or discrimination. However, I don’t think enough thought is given to what LGBTQ+ actually want (if anything) as users of AI.”

Taylor emphasizes, from scholar José Esteban Muñoz, “ _Queerness is essentially about the rejection of a here and now and an insistence on potentiality or concrete possibility for another world._ ”

The study itself reads that,

> “Prior research has demonstrated that participation in online fan communities, such as through writing fan fiction, empowers LGBTQ+ individuals to challenge dominant narratives by creating alternate worlds and possibilities.”

The authors in the study observe the use of collaborative technology, research known as computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW).

> “CSCW scholarship emphasizes how queer communities utilize digital spaces to engage in artistic expression as a means of collective identity affirmation and social support.”

Through social experiments and thorough research of queer history, trans and queer online communities, and LGBTQ+ artistic work, CSCW researchers explain the effects of generative AI on the lives and labor of queer creators.

> “The rise of GenAI has led to fears of unauthorized use of original content to train models and has flooded spaces with AI-generated material.”

The study starts by mentioning the history of queer art through Keith Haring, a gay man who fought stigmatization of AIDS during the epidemic in the 1980s and 1990s, and how an impactful art piece of his was scraped via the use of generative AI by a troll on the internet.

> “We find that participants’ queer artistic practices are deeply relational and anti-capitalist. Participants juxtaposed the relationality of their art with the perceived anti-relationality of GenAI development and use, such as facilitating worker exploitation.”
>
>
>
> “Muñoz conceptualizes utopia not as an abstract future, but as a tangible response to the recognition that ‘something is missing’ in the present. Art thus becomes a vehicle for queer world-making, such as the queer intimacy depicted in Frank O’Hara’s poetry and ephemeral performances like drag and punk shows.”

Taylor relays that when they interviewed queer artists for this study, “their primary concerns were not social biases but rather the ways that generative AI harms queer artistic communities.”

According to the study’s article, one of their participants said,“‘ _I don’t put my art online anymore. I don’t want [fast fashion brand] stealing it. I don’t want AI combing through it to take chunks of it and cut it apart and use it for other things I don’t want. I don’t want any of that. So I purely share my art person to person,’"._

Jordan Taylor told _The Needle_ that if AI were to be utilized in a way that protects queer artists,

> “I see it in small models that can run on a laptop, models that are bizarre, glitchy, or ‘bad’ [because] they are not designed to create realistic or high-fidelity images. They may require less training data, so you can be more thoughtful about where data comes from. These models may also require less computational power to train or run, making them more sustainable.”

Generative AI appears to exploit queer art, while LGBTQ+ communities aim to develop the thought that goes into their queer identities and their artistic labor at the same time.

Niche fandoms like the virtual space of yaoi on the internet have led to the exploration of gender and sexuality among transgender fans, inspiring trans artists and allowing queer collaborators to meet and form communities, create projects, and further their artistic journeys.

The anthology AMERICAN *FUJO* is put together by a collective of artists who share similar experiences discovering queer realities utilizing art and virtual space.

Directly from the anthology website, a contributor Elliot Asher will use “ _psychoanalytic theory to theorize through the fantasy of forced transition, deconstructing what we might mean when we say or feel that ‘yaoi made me trans._ ’”

The creators Alexis Rippen and tshirt3000 state on the website about how their project conceptualizes the journey of gender expression and exploring individual sexuality through fandom.

> “We organized 17 skilled creators, with 13 writers and 5 comic creators to take part in this expedition.”

The selection of writers and artists they organized created pieces based on prompts regarding trans identity and the idea of being a fujoshi, whether said creators were trans, fujoshi, both, or neither.

> "We are interested in celebrating the rotten, the pointless, the meaningless—the queer,”

They explain where the terms fujoshi [“‘ _rotten girl_ ’”] and yaoi [“‘ _no climax, no point, no meaning_ ’”] come from: derogatory Japanese verbiage that refers to the genre of Boy’s Love and its generalized women and girl fans.

> “Japanese fans instead use BL, or Boys' Love, to denote the same comics that we might refer to as yaoi in the Anglosphere.”

The project has currently concluded its second wave of pre-orders and is not out yet, but it is stated to be structured by “clusters and questions” surrounding gender, sexuality, power, and virtual space.

Artists, often queer, have been opposed to generative AI for all that it exploits from queer labor and the artistic spaces it pervades.

Trans and queer identities are expressed through art, shared with their community, and preserved through art when society tries to limit queer potential.

Regardless of generative AI's existence, LGBTQ+ artists have shown that they will create space to be heard and understood in their own communities.

Jordan Taylor also mentioned that queer artists tend to lean towards glitchy or camp design, and generative AI, if it has a place in spaces that trans and queer individuals occupy, should be limited to a controlled system based on art that assists queer potential without exploiting queer labor.
external.title: Queer Artists Continue To Resist GenerativeAI and Build Spaces To Share Themselves

The study, written by authors Jordan Taylor, Joel Mire, Alicia DeVrio, Maarten Sap, Haiyi Zhu, and Sarah E. Fox, details how individuals of queer, trans and nonbinary communities feel about the rise of generative AI. 

Ranging from game design, writing anthologies, and cosplay construction, to digital art trades, fan-made art books, and media design, queer artists from a range of different backgrounds come together to share their art. 

Studies show that the history of trans and queer art influences what we create in present times, and the origins of queer art make sense of how generative AI affects the communities formed by LGBTQ+ art in the present. 

When asked what made him question the impact of generative AI on queer artists, Jordan Taylor told The Needle via email that,

“Researchers tend to think of LGBTQ+ communities as targets of bias or discrimination. However, I don’t think enough thought is given to what LGBTQ+ actually want (if anything) as users of AI.”

Taylor emphasizes, from scholar José Esteban Muñoz, “Queerness is essentially about the rejection of a here and now and an insistence on potentiality or concrete possibility for another world.” 

The study itself reads that,

“Prior research has demonstrated that participation in online fan communities, such as through writing fan fiction, empowers LGBTQ+ individuals to challenge dominant narratives by creating alternate worlds and possibilities.” 

The authors in the study observe the use of collaborative technology, research known as computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW). 

“CSCW scholarship emphasizes how queer communities utilize digital spaces to engage in artistic expression as a means of collective identity affirmation and social support.” 

Through social experiments and thorough research of queer history, trans and queer online communities, and LGBTQ+ artistic work, CSCW researchers explain the effects of generative AI on the lives and labor of queer creators. 

 “The rise of GenAI has led to fears of unauthorized use of original content to train models and has flooded spaces with AI-generated material.” 

The study starts by mentioning the history of queer art through Keith Haring, a gay man who fought stigmatization of AIDS during the epidemic in the 1980s and 1990s, and how an impactful art piece of his was scraped via the use of generative AI by a troll on the internet.

“We find that participants’ queer artistic practices are deeply relational and anti-capitalist. Participants juxtaposed the relationality of their art with the perceived anti-relationality of GenAI development and use, such as facilitating worker exploitation.”   



“Muñoz conceptualizes utopia not as an abstract future, but as a tangible response to the recognition that ‘something is missing’ in the present. Art thus becomes a vehicle for queer world-making, such as the queer intimacy depicted in Frank O’Hara’s poetry and ephemeral performances like drag and punk shows.” 

Taylor relays that when they interviewed queer artists for this study, “their primary concerns were not social biases but rather the ways that generative AI harms queer artistic communities.” 

According to the study’s article, one of their participants said,“‘I don’t put my art online anymore. I don’t want [fast fashion brand] stealing it. I don’t want AI combing through it to take chunks of it and cut it apart and use it for other things I don’t want. I don’t want any of that. So I purely share my art person to person,’".

Jordan Taylor told The Needle that if AI were to be utilized in a way that protects queer artists,

“I see it in small models that can run on a laptop, models that are bizarre, glitchy, or ‘bad’ [because] they are not designed to create realistic or high-fidelity images. They may require less training data, so you can be more thoughtful about where data comes from. These models may also require less computational power to train or run, making them more sustainable.” 

Generative AI appears to exploit queer art, while LGBTQ+ communities aim to develop the thought that goes into their queer identities and their artistic labor at the same time. 

Niche fandoms like the virtual space of yaoi on the internet have led to the exploration of gender and sexuality among transgender fans, inspiring trans artists and allowing queer collaborators to meet and form communities, create projects, and further their artistic journeys. 

The anthology AMERICAN *FUJO* is put together by a collective of artists who share similar experiences discovering queer realities utilizing art and virtual space. 

Directly from the anthology website, a contributor Elliot Asher will use “psychoanalytic theory to theorize through the fantasy of forced transition, deconstructing what we might mean when we say or feel that ‘yaoi made me trans.’” 

The creators Alexis Rippen and tshirt3000 state on the website about how their project conceptualizes the journey of gender expression and exploring individual sexuality through fandom. 

“We organized 17 skilled creators, with 13 writers and 5 comic creators to take part in this expedition.” 

The selection of writers and artists they organized created pieces based on prompts regarding trans identity and the idea of being a fujoshi, whether said creators were trans, fujoshi, both, or neither. 

"We are interested in celebrating the rotten, the pointless, the meaningless—the queer,” 

They explain where the terms fujoshi [“‘rotten girl’”] and yaoi [“‘no climax, no point, no meaning’”] come from: derogatory Japanese verbiage that refers to the genre of Boy’s Love and its generalized women and girl fans. 

“Japanese fans instead use BL, or Boys' Love, to denote the same comics that we might refer to as yaoi in the Anglosphere.” 

The project has currently concluded its second wave of pre-orders and is not out yet, but it is stated to be structured by “clusters and questions” surrounding gender, sexuality, power, and virtual space. 

Artists, often queer, have been opposed to generative AI for all that it exploits from queer labor and the artistic spaces it pervades. 

Trans and queer identities are expressed through art, shared with their community, and preserved through art when society tries to limit queer potential.  

Regardless of generative AI's existence, LGBTQ+ artists have shown that they will create space to be heard and understood in their own communities. 

Jordan Taylor also mentioned that queer artists tend to lean towards glitchy or camp design, and generative AI, if it has a place in spaces that trans and queer individuals occupy, should be limited to a controlled system based on art that assists queer potential without exploiting queer labor.

By Catesby Holmes

This article is a republication from Rewire News Group. The original release can be found here.

In “The Fleeing Season,” Jamie Brooks rebukes the injustices of modern American childhood: “I didn’t grow up with gun violence in that way.”

People in the U.S. “are not living in freedom,” Brooks said. “They’re living in fear.”Jamie D. Brooks/Cage Rivera/Rewire News Group

Jamie Brooks considers herself a reproductive justice migrant.

In 2021, she and her husband uprooted their family from a Maryland suburb outside D.C. and moved to England. Officially, the move was a professional one: Brooks’ husband is a journalist at _Bloomberg_ , and he was offered a position in the London bureau.

But, for Brooks—a Black woman with three small children—the decision was profoundly and painfully personal.

When Brooks began thinking about leaving the United States, the COVID-19 pandemic was raging, and she worked as a health-care attorney at a hospital. George Floyd had been murdered by police. The Trump administration was separating migrant families and teargassing protesters. The drumbeat of mass shootings, which had slowed in the early, isolated months of the pandemic, was resuming its steady tempo.

She couldn’t escape the conclusion that in the U.S., she couldn’t keep her kids safe.

Americans “are not living in freedom. They’re living in fear,” she said in an interview with _Rewire News Group_.

Brooks’ new memoir, The Fleeing Season (out Nov. 17, 2026), traces her family’s decision to leave the country for safer shores, and examines whether they’ve found it in the United Kingdom, a country that presents its own challenges for a mixed-race immigrant family.

I interviewed Brooks about the primal fears of motherhood and her complicated relationship with the U.S.—one that’s now tinged with an unfamiliar shade: political hope.

_This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity._

**Your story is, in some respects, a familiar one: A mother flees her homeland to give her kids a better future. But it complicates that narrative. For one thing, you left a country that many immigrants are still literally dying to reach. You write that your migration journey was shaped by your race and gender.**

I had a very privileged life in the U.S., even as a Black female. On paper, I had all of the trappings of what would look like a stable, successful life.

But I would have these moments, when you get hit with racism or colorism. That’s always jarring.

That’s just the nature of these shells we grow up in. [Race and gender define] how you get treated, and what you get exposed to, and how the world treats you.

It’s a lens that I can’t strip away. I will always see the world [as a Black woman] because I am seen as that. As soon as I step out anywhere, that’s how people see me.

**Your story is also different from another popular media portrayal of modern migration—that of the “digital nomad.” These are white-collar, remote workers, often young and single, who move abroad for a more flexible, affordable lifestyle. That’s not why you moved your family to England. What were you looking for?**

Safety, safety, safety, safety.

When you come into parenthood, there’s a biological freakout. Your mind gets rewired. There’s this matrescence thing that happens, and everything’s about safety and protecting these kids.

[Over time] for a lot of us, it starts to soften a bit. [Yet] as my kids were getting older, and I was watching what was happening with the treatment of people at the border and gun violence, that fear wasn’t subsiding. I just couldn’t shake that perpetual state of anxiety. …

Inequity was growing. Access to health care was becoming more difficult … And I didn’t grow up with gun violence in that way—the mass gun violence. … I wasn’t afraid of being shot and killed going to high school.

**Motherhood, gun violence, racism, and abortion may seem like separate issues to many people. Can you tease out the relationship you see between them?**

It was an evolution in thought. [At first], I don’t think I was thinking about these issues as reproductive justice issues. If you’re parenting [small children], it really is day to day—just get this kid … to put their shoe on, let’s get out the door.

The physical nature of parenting eases up a little bit as they get older. And having conversations with friends about what was happening politically, socially—it all started to come into that third realm of reproductive justice: I should have a right to raise my kids in a safe environment. … The gun violence [was] bananas to me.

And then abortion: … It clicked for me once I started working for Planned Parenthood.

I’d never done enterprise risk for a health organization or hospital where I had to worry about the safety of each and every single employee. … Are they safe coming to and from work? Are they safe going home?

Wherever you fall on the spectrum [of reproductive health care], I can disagree with you. You can disagree with me. But that terrorism and violence is accepted as part of this [political debate] is unacceptable to me. It’s inexcusable.

It all seems connected to me. Whether you’re going to parent or not parent … we should be able to do [it] without the threat of violence and terror and killing people.

**You call yourself a “reproductive justice migrant.” Why do you think that’s a helpful term?**

We talk often about the right to have a child [and] the right not to have a child. … I don’t feel like we talk often [enough about] the right to parent the children we have in safe and healthy environments.

If you’re scared to go to school because somebody might bring a gun one day, or somebody recently brought a gun to school and shot other kids three states away, this is not a safe and healthy environment.

We have to lift this [truth] up. I think this is how we make change.

**Do you try to explain that to Brits who ask why you came there?**

I do. And people are really shocked. They say, _Well, there’s not that much gun violence, is there?_

And no, it’s not like every time you step out your door, there’s bullets flying. But it’s the anxiety of you never know where, you never know when. It’s always a possibility. … [That’s] not freedom. We call it freedom, but people are not living in freedom. They’re living in fear that’s constricting so much of what we naturally do, which is unfair.

It doesn’t have to be that way.

**Do you have hard conversations with your kids about your decision to move abroad?**

We are very honest with them.

We weren’t when we came; they were 3, 5, and 7 [years old] … But as they’ve gotten older, particularly when we make these trips back across the ocean, we started to be honest with them, [especially] about gun violence.

We wanted them to look at the extent that mass gun violence is still happening in the U.S. … and go, “That’s so crazy. I don’t understand it.” Rather than [feel] this is just part of who we are, and it’s unfair. I want them to not understand it. …

[We aim for] balance: [The United States is] this wonderful, amazing place. We have people we love. We need to go [visit]—and yeah, they are tearing people off the streets and kidnapping them. They see all that. They read the news, so it’s hard.

**I’m hearing you talk more about gun violence than about abortion bans, but you write in the book that your mother was skeptical about your move abroad—until the** **_Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_** **decision that ended federal abortion protections in 2022. What did that ruling change in her?**

It was such a moving moment for me. I’d spent all this time working in reproductive justice, and … she never was like, “I’m so glad you’re working on that.” … There was no commentary.

But then [after _Dobbs_], it [became] very clear that this was something she felt passionately about. … There was this fear that this right, this bodily autonomy had been taken away from so many people.

That must have been the straw that broke the camel’s back. … to see something so tangible potentially taken away from so many people.

I think she was terrified. I mean, I know she was: I could see it in her face. She kept saying, “It’s like the _Handmaid’s Tale_. This is where we are headed.”

She only has daughters and granddaughters … the reality of being women and birthing people that, I think, terrified her.

**Working in hospitals, you’ve seen other reproductive injustices up close: gunshot wounds, birth complications, sexual abuse survivors, trafficked teens. How did that professional experience inform your personal perspective?**

Seeing these pockets of extreme injustice—whether it’s people not having access to care, being a victim of trafficking, or being a victim of sexual violence or exploitation—I don’t feel like I was having a lot of conversations [at the time] about how this is all a reproductive injustice.

[But] if you peel back the layers on it, all these things are part of the onion. I just don’t think they can be separated. I think it’s all linked. I think it’s the way that we view individual freedoms and who we fight for, who we advocate for, who’s it’s okay that they’re victims, what bodies we don’t value. I think it’s all part of it.

**Do you feel that you’ve achieved what you were looking for as a mother, as a Black woman, by taking your family to England?**

Yes and no.

We have a better baseline [here]. … We believe in universal health-care coverage. It’s shabby. It’s threadbare. It’s being sold off piecemeal and privatized. But in general, most people think that we should have that.

In general, most people think that we shouldn’t have unfettered access to guns.

…[We have] paid maternity leave and paternity leave. … If my kids or their partners decide to pursue parenthood, there’s still that mechanism in place.

So yeah, there’s a better baseline. … It feels like we jumped to a lily pad that feels a little bit bigger and safer.

… It’s not Valhalla. It feels safer, but it all feels tenuous. … There’s still the rise of the far right. There’s still large anti-immigrant sentiment all over this country.

I’m in a mixed race marriage. My husband’s white. I think people perceive him as an expat. He’s American; he came with his job. But I think just on sight I’m viewed as a migrant. … When you look on the ground, at what’s happening here and where the anti-immigrant sentiment is focused, it is not on Ukrainian refugees [or] American expats. …

The focus is on people who look like me. I feel that for sure. It’s very palpable.

**We are speaking just days after the 2026 midterm election. How are you feeling about U.S. politics and Texas, where you have deep ties?**

I’m super excited. It’s one of those moments where you’re like, _Oh, I wish I was there to celebrate and_ _live in the glory of it_.

I’m so grateful for young people in Texas right now. … I feel like that’s going to give the youth there what so many of them haven’t had. We’ve had these highs and lows. [Kids] really haven’t.

I know that they’re going to be busy working—the other side. We’ve got to roll up our sleeves and get to work. It’s still not going to be easy. But I’m hopeful. Hopeful!

She couldn’t escape the conclusion that in the U.S., she couldn’t keep her kids safe.

But I would have these moments, when you get hit with racism or colorism. That’s always jarring.

That’s just the nature of these shells we grow up in. [Race and gender define] how you get treated, and what you get exposed to, and how the world treats you.

It’s a lens that I can’t strip away. I will always see the world [as a Black woman] because I am seen as that. As soon as I step out anywhere, that’s how people see me.

**Your story is also different from another popular media portrayal of modern migration—that of the “digital nomad.” These are white-collar, remote workers, often young and single, who move abroad for a more flexible, affordable lifestyle. That’s not why you moved your family to England. What were you looking for?**

When you come into parenthood, there’s a biological freakout. Your mind gets rewired. There’s this matrescence thing that happens, and everything’s about safety and protecting these kids.

[Over time] for a lot of us, it starts to soften a bit. [Yet] as my kids were getting older, and I was watching what was happening with the treatment of people at the border and gun violence, that fear wasn’t subsiding. I just couldn’t shake that perpetual state of anxiety. …

Inequity was growing. Access to health care was becoming more difficult … And I didn’t grow up with gun violence in that way—the mass gun violence. … I wasn’t afraid of being shot and killed going to high school.

I’d never done enterprise risk for a health organization or hospital where I had to worry about the safety of each and every single employee. … Are they safe coming to and from work? Are they safe going home?

It all seems connected to me. Whether you’re going to parent or not parent … we should be able to do [it] without the threat of violence and terror and killing people.

If you’re scared to go to school because somebody might bring a gun one day, or somebody recently brought a gun to school and shot other kids three states away, this is not a safe and healthy environment.

We have to lift this [truth] up. I think this is how we make change.

We call it freedom, but people are not living in freedom. They’re living in fear that’s constricting so much of what we naturally do, which is unfair.

I think she was terrified. I mean, I know she was: I could see it in her face. She kept saying, “It’s like the _Handmaid’s Tale_. This is where we are headed.”
